question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Triumph
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Defeat.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Triumph" means a great victory or achievement; a feeling of great happiness or satisfaction resulting from success. (विजय / जीत)
◦ Example: The team celebrated their triumph after winning the championship.

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Defeat", meaning failure to win or succeed; being overcome by an opponent. (हार / पराजय)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Capture (पकड़ना): To take control of a person, place or thing by force; not an antonym of triumph.

• Option 3: Attainment (उपलब्धि): The achievement of a goal; this is actually close in meaning to triumph, not opposite to it.

• Option 4: Succeed (सफल होना): To achieve an aim or purpose; this is a synonym of triumph (used as a verb), not its antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of Triumph: victory, conquest, success, win.

• Other common antonym pairs tested in SSC: Victory × Defeat, Success × Failure, Glory × Disgrace.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
Ranen feels that the notion of democracy is a farce.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Reality.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Notion" means a belief, idea or view held by someone about something, often without being based on solid proof. (धारणा / विचार)
◦ Example: He had a strange notion that the earth was flat.

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Reality", meaning the state of things as they actually exist, as opposed to an idea or belief about them. (वास्तविकता / सच्चाई)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Quotient (भागफल): A result obtained by dividing one quantity by another; unrelated in meaning to notion.

• Option 2: Law (कानून): A system of rules; not an antonym of notion.

• Option 4: Portion (भाग/हिस्सा): A part of something; not related in meaning to notion.

NOTE

• Synonyms of Notion: idea, belief, view, opinion, conception.

• Other similar antonym pairs: Fact × Fiction, Belief × Fact/Reality, Illusion × Reality.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Wax
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Wane.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Wax" (used as a verb) means to increase gradually in size, strength or intensity, as the moon does between new moon and full moon. (बढ़ना / वृद्धि होना)
◦ Example: His enthusiasm for the project began to wax as the deadline approached.

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Wane", meaning to decrease gradually in size, strength or intensity. (घटना / क्षीण होना)
◦ Example: Interest in the old traditions began to wane over the years.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Polish (चमकाना): To make something smooth and shiny by rubbing; unrelated to wax as a verb of increase.

• Option 2: Cane (छड़ी/बेंत): A stick, or to beat with a stick; unrelated in meaning.

• Option 3: Wail (विलाप करना): To cry out in grief or pain; unrelated in meaning to wax.

NOTE

• The expression "wax and wane" is commonly used to describe the moon's phases and, figuratively, anything that alternately grows and shrinks.

• Other tricky homophone-like pairs tested in SSC: Wax (मोम/बढ़ना) vs Wane (घटना); Ebb (घटना, ज्वार का उतार) vs Flow (बहना, ज्वार का चढ़ाव).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Pattron.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word is incorrectly spelt as "Pattron"; the correct spelling is "Patron" — a person who gives financial or other support to a person, cause, or activity, or a regular customer of a shop/restaurant.
◦ Example: The art gallery found a generous patron to fund the new exhibition.

• Spelling key: PA + TRON, with a single "t". The double "t" in "Pattron" is the error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Connotation" — correctly spelt; it means an idea or feeling that a word invokes in addition to its literal meaning.

• Option 3: "Dearth" — correctly spelt; it means a scarcity or lack of something.

• Option 4: "Quarry" — correctly spelt; it means an open excavation for extracting stone, or an animal/person being hunted.

NOTE

• Related word: patronage (the support given by a patron), patronize (to support, or to treat condescendingly).

• Other commonly misspelt words tested in SSC: Occurrence, Embarrass, Questionnaire, Millennium, Rhythm.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
She was upset seeing the scattered documents.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Gathered.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Scattered" means thrown or spread over a wide area in a random or disorderly way. (बिखरा हुआ)
◦ Example: Papers were scattered all over the floor after the wind blew through the window.

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Gathered", meaning brought together into one place or group; collected. (इकट्ठा किया हुआ)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Perished (नष्ट होना): To die or be destroyed; not related in meaning to scattered.

• Option 2: Dissipated (तितर-बितर होना): To scatter or disperse; this is actually a synonym of scattered, not its antonym.

• Option 3: Sprinkled (छिड़कना): To scatter something in small drops or particles; again close to a synonym, not the antonym.

NOTE

• Synonyms of Scattered: dispersed, strewn, spread out, dissipated.

• Other similar antonym pairs: Scatter × Collect/Gather, Disperse × Assemble, Strewn × Arranged.

question:
Select the grammatically correct sentence.
A. The Supriya is the best girl in the class.
B. Supriya is the best girl in the class.
C. Supriya is best girl in the class.
D. The Supriya is a best girl in the class.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. B.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Proper nouns and the article "the": A proper noun (a specific name of a person, like "Supriya") does not normally take the definite article "the" before it.
◦ Correct: Supriya is...
◦ Incorrect: The Supriya is...

• Rule — Superlative degree: When a superlative adjective (e.g. "best") is used to compare one thing/person with the rest of a definite group, it must be preceded by the definite article "the".
◦ Correct: Supriya is the best girl in the class.
◦ Incorrect: Supriya is best girl in the class.

• Applying both rules together, the only sentence that correctly omits "the" before the proper noun "Supriya" and correctly includes "the" before the superlative "best" is: "Supriya is the best girl in the class."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (C): "Supriya is best girl in the class" is incorrect because the article "the" is missing before the superlative "best".

• Option 2 (A): "The Supriya is the best girl in the class" is incorrect because the article "the" is wrongly used before the proper noun "Supriya".

• Option 3 (D): "The Supriya is a best girl in the class" is incorrect on two counts — "the" is wrongly used before the proper noun, and the indefinite article "a" cannot be used before a superlative form like "best".

NOTE

• Proper nouns take "the" only in specific cases — e.g. names of rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, newspapers, and some countries (the Ganga, the Alps, the Times of India, the United States) — but not before ordinary personal names.

• Superlative adjectives (best, tallest, most beautiful, etc.) are almost always preceded by "the" when comparing within a definite group.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
You are the ______ to the throne and should behave in such a manner.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. heir.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "heir" means a person legally entitled to the property or rank of another on that person's death; a person who inherits a position or title.
◦ Example: The prince is the heir to the throne.

• The sentence talks about someone entitled to inherit "the throne", so the correct word is "heir", not any of its homophones.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "hair" — refers to the strands that grow on the skin/scalp; it is a homophone of "heir" but does not fit the meaning of the sentence.

• Option 2: "here" — an adverb of place, meaning "in this place"; it does not fit grammatically or in meaning.

• Option 3: "hare" — refers to an animal similar to a rabbit; it is a homophone of "heir" but unrelated in meaning.

NOTE

• Homophones are words that sound alike but differ in spelling and meaning. Other commonly confused homophone sets in SSC: their/there/they're, its/it's, to/too/two, whose/who's, principal/principle.

• The related word "heiress" refers to a female heir, especially to a large fortune.

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
Pudding had already been prepared by her.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. She had already prepared pudding.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Pudding had already been prepared by her" is in the Passive Voice, Past Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + had + been + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + had + V3 + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "her" (object of "by") becomes the subject "She"; the auxiliary "had" is retained as it is; the past participle "been prepared" is converted to the past participle form of the main verb, "prepared"; and "pudding" becomes the object.
◦ Active: She had already prepared pudding.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "has already prepared" is the active form of the Present Perfect Tense, not the Past Perfect Tense used in the given sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "have" does not agree with the third-person singular subject "She"; it should be "has" or "had", and in any case the tense is wrong.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will prepare" is the Simple Future Tense, which does not correspond to the Past Perfect Tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• The marker word "already", along with the structure "had + been + V3", is a strong indicator of the Past Perfect Passive form.

• Sequence of tense: when converting Past Perfect Passive to Active, the auxiliary "had" always stays the same in the active sentence.

question: Describe how you will tell your parents that Darshana was laughed at by all her classmates in active voice.
option_1: All her classmates laughed at Darshana.
option_2: All her classmates laughing at Darshana.
option_3: Darshana is laughed at by all her classmates.
option_4: All her classmates will been laugh at Darshana.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. All her classmates laughed at Darshana.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Darshana was laughed at by all her classmates" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense, using the phrasal verb "laugh at".

• Rule — Simple Past Tense (with phrasal verb):
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + preposition + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + preposition + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "all her classmates" becomes the subject; the verb "was laughed at" is converted to its simple past active form "laughed at" (keeping the preposition "at" with the phrasal verb); and "Darshana" becomes the object.
◦ Active: All her classmates laughed at Darshana.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2 is incorrect because "laughing" (present participle, without any auxiliary verb) does not form a complete, grammatically correct finite verb for a simple past statement.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it merely repeats the sentence in the Passive Voice (with "is" instead of "was"), rather than converting it to Active Voice.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "will been laugh" is not a grammatically valid verb form in English at all.

NOTE

• With phrasal/prepositional verbs like "laugh at", "look after", "listen to", the preposition must stay attached to the verb in both active and passive conversions.

• Keep the tense identical between the active and passive versions — only the voice changes, not the time reference.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. "Well, you can't make me", she said, looking back at me.
B. She went on, "Well, you might try", I responded, and she laughed.
C. She came in and we said hello, then she just looked at me and said, "What do you want?" McKechnie remembered.
D. "Well, I want you to grin and seem pleased", I added.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. CDAB.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A coherent paragraph must open with the sentence that sets the scene and introduces the speakers, and then follow the natural back-and-forth of the conversation in logical order.

• Sentence C is the best opener — it introduces the scene ("She came in and we said hello...") and starts the dialogue with "What do you want?"

• Sentence D logically follows C, as it is the direct reply to "What do you want?" — "Well, I want you to grin and seem pleased".

• Sentence A follows next, as her response to being asked to grin and seem pleased — "Well, you can't make me".

• Sentence B concludes the paragraph, continuing the dialogue with "Well, you might try" and the reaction ("I responded, and she laughed").

• Hence, the coherent order is: C — D — A — B.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ACBD) is incorrect because it begins with sentence A, which is a reply ("you can't make me") and cannot logically be the opening line without any context.

• Option 2 (DCBA) is incorrect because it begins with D, which is itself a response to a question ("What do you want?") that has not yet been asked.

• Option 3 (BCDA) is incorrect because it begins with B, which refers back to something ("she went on") that requires a preceding statement already made.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, look for the sentence that introduces the subject/scene without using pronouns that need an antecedent (like "she", "it", "this") — that sentence is usually the opening sentence.

• Words like "went on", "added", "responded" are strong clues that the sentence continues an earlier statement, and such sentences cannot be the first sentence of the paragraph.

question:
Sentences of a paragraph are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the sentences in the correct order to form a meaningful and coherent paragraph.
A. After examining these three approaches carefully I crossed the bridge and examined the Kedarnath pilgrim road for half a mile.
B. There were three approaches to the bridge; one from the north, one from the south and between these two a well-beaten footpath from the Rudraprayag bazaar.
C. Satisfied that the leopard had not crossed the river, I determined to put in operation my plan for closing the two bridges at night and thus confining the leopard to my side of the river.
D. Next, I examined the footpath on which three nights previously my goat had been killed.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. BADC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A coherent paragraph must begin with the sentence that introduces the main subject clearly, without relying on pronouns or references established earlier.

• Sentence B is the natural opener — it introduces "three approaches to the bridge", giving the reader the necessary background before any of them are examined.

• Sentence A follows logically, as it refers back to "these three approaches" mentioned in B, and describes the writer crossing the bridge and examining the Kedarnath pilgrim road.

• Sentence D comes next, introduced by the connector "Next", describing the examination of the footpath where the goat was killed.

• Sentence C concludes the paragraph, as the writer, now "satisfied" after all the examinations described in A and D, decides on his plan of action.

• Hence, the coherent order is: B — A — D — C.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DABC) is incorrect because it begins with D, which uses the connector "Next", implying that something has already been described before it.

• Option 2 (CDAB) is incorrect because it begins with C, the concluding/summarising sentence ("Satisfied that..."), which cannot logically come first.

• Option 3 (ABCD) is incorrect because it begins with A, which refers to "these three approaches" — a phrase that requires the prior introduction found in sentence B.

NOTE

• Look out for back-referencing phrases like "these three approaches", "next", "satisfied that..." — such phrases almost always indicate that the sentence cannot be the opening line of the paragraph.

• The opening sentence of a para-jumble usually introduces a new subject/scene in general terms, without demonstrative or anaphoric references.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word.
The patient found the doctor to be obtuse and distracted by constant calls on his phone.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. astute.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Obtuse" means slow to understand or perceive; not sharp-witted or perceptive; dull. (मंदबुद्धि / सुस्त)
◦ Example: He was too obtuse to grasp the hidden meaning of her remark.

• Its most appropriate antonym is "Astute", meaning having or showing an ability to accurately assess situations and turn this to one's advantage; sharp-witted and shrewd. (चतुर / तीक्ष्णबुद्धि)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Obese (मोटा/स्थूल): Very overweight; relates to body size, not intelligence, and is unrelated to obtuse.

• Option 3: Banal (सामान्य/उबाऊ): Lacking originality; boring due to overuse; not an antonym of obtuse.

• Option 4: Obsolete (अप्रचलित): No longer in use or practised; outdated; unrelated in meaning to obtuse.

NOTE

• Synonyms of Obtuse: dull, dim-witted, slow, imperceptive.

• Other similar antonym pairs tested in SSC: Astute × Naive, Shrewd × Gullible, Perceptive × Obtuse.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select 'No substitution'.
He was so curious that he rose many questions in the meeting.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. that he raised many questions.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Rise vs Raise: "Rise" is an intransitive verb (does not take a direct object) meaning to move upward or get up on its own; its past tense is "rose". "Raise" is a transitive verb (takes a direct object) meaning to lift or bring something up; its past tense is "raised".

• Since the sentence has a direct object, "questions", that is being brought up, the correct transitive verb is "raise" (past tense "raised"), not the intransitive "rise".

• Also, "questions" is a countable noun and takes "many", not "much" (used for uncountable nouns).

• Applying both corrections: "that he raised many questions".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "that he rose much questions" is incorrect because it retains the wrong verb "rose" (intransitive) and also wrongly uses "much" with the countable noun "questions".

• Option 3: "that he aroused many questions" is incorrect because "aroused" means to awaken a feeling or reaction (e.g. arouse suspicion/interest), which does not correctly collocate with "questions" in the sense of putting them forward.

• Option 4: "No substitution" is incorrect because the original sentence contains a clear verb error ("rose" used transitively) that must be corrected.

NOTE

• Similar intransitive/transitive confusable pairs tested in SSC: Lie (to recline) × Lay (to place something); Sit × Set; Fall × Fell.

• Standard collocation to remember: "to raise a question/point/issue" — always with "raise", never "rise".

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Carolina opened a savings account to save money for later.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. for a rainy day.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to save for a rainy day" means to save money for a possible time of need in the future, in case of difficulties or hard times. (भविष्य के बुरे समय के लिए बचत करना)
◦ Example: He always puts aside a portion of his salary to save for a rainy day.

• The underlined segment "money for later" conveys exactly this idea of saving for a future uncertain time, so it is best substituted by the idiomatic expression "for a rainy day".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "for a cold day" — not an established English idiom; it does not convey the intended meaning.

• Option 3: "for a sunny day" — not an idiom; a sunny day usually connotes something pleasant, not a time of need, so it contradicts the intended meaning.

• Option 4: "for a hot day" — not an established idiom and does not convey the meaning of saving for future hardship.

NOTE

• The idiom draws on the image of rain (bad weather) representing hard times, when one would need savings to fall back on.

• Other savings/money-related idioms common in SSC: "to make ends meet" (to have just enough money to live on), "to feather one's nest" (to accumulate wealth, often selfishly), "penny wise, pound foolish" (careful with small amounts but wasteful with large ones).

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution of the given group of words.
A similarity between like features of two things, on which a comparison may be based.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Analogy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Analogy" means a similarity between like features of two things, on which a comparison may be based. (सादृश्य / समानता)
◦ Example: The teacher used an analogy between the human heart and a pump to explain how blood circulates.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Amalgamation (मिश्रण/विलय): The combining or uniting of two or more things into one; not related to comparison/similarity.

• Option 3: Apathy (उदासीनता): A lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern; unrelated to the given meaning.

• Option 4: Ambiguity (अस्पष्टता): The quality of being open to more than one interpretation; unrelated to the given meaning.

NOTE

• Related word: Analogous (adjective) — similar or comparable in certain respects.

• Other one-word substitutions often confused with "Analogy": Metaphor (an implied comparison, a figure of speech), Simile (an explicit comparison using "like" or "as").

question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
Do not beat about the bush when you have anything to say.
option_4: To avoid giving a definite answer or position
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To avoid giving a definite answer or position.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "to beat about the bush" means to avoid talking about what is important; to speak indirectly or evasively instead of getting straight to the point. (घुमा-फिराकर बात करना / मुद्दे से बचना)
◦ Example: Stop beating about the bush and tell me exactly what happened.

• Among the given options, "To avoid giving a definite answer or position" best captures this sense of evasiveness and indirectness.

• The idiom originates from hunting, where beaters would strike bushes to flush out birds/game without directly entering the bush themselves — i.e., approaching the goal indirectly.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "To try to influence" — this describes persuasion, not evasiveness; it does not match the idiom's meaning.

• Option 2: "To shift blame on others" — this describes deflecting responsibility, which is a different idea from speaking indirectly.

• Option 3: "To argue" — this describes a disagreement or dispute, which is unrelated to the idea of avoiding the main point.

NOTE

• A closely related idiom with the opposite sense: "to come straight to the point" / "to call a spade a spade" — to speak directly and plainly.

• Other idioms of evasiveness tested in SSC: "to hedge one's bets", "to sit on the fence", "to pussyfoot around".

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Abendance.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word is incorrectly spelt as "Abendance"; the correct spelling is "Abundance" — a very large quantity of something; plentifulness.
◦ Example: The region is known for its abundance of natural resources.

• Spelling key: A + BUN + DANCE. The letter "u" in the second syllable ("bun") is missing in the incorrect form "Abendance", where it has wrongly been written as "e".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Astute" — correctly spelt; it means shrewd, sharp-witted.

• Option 2: "Absolute" — correctly spelt; it means complete, total, unrestricted.

• Option 3: "Abrupt" — correctly spelt; it means sudden and unexpected.

NOTE

• Related word: abundant (adjective) — existing or available in large quantities.

• Other commonly misspelt "a-" words tested in SSC: Accommodate, Acquaintance, Acknowledgement, Acquire, Absence.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
The money paid to former wife, husband or partner when the marriage is ended.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Alimony.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Alimony" means the money that a person is legally required to pay to their former wife, husband, or partner after a divorce or separation. (गुज़ारा भत्ता)
◦ Example: The court ordered him to pay alimony to his former wife every month.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Compensation (क्षतिपूर्ति): Money paid to someone as recompense for loss, injury, or suffering; a broader term, not specific to former spouses.

• Option 3: Recompense (प्रतिकर/मुआवज़ा): Something given in return for a loss or service, similar to compensation but not specifically related to marriage/divorce.

• Option 4: Maintenance (भरण-पोषण): A general term for financial support (e.g., for a spouse or child), but it is broader than "alimony", which specifically refers to post-divorce spousal support.

NOTE

• Related legal terms often confused in SSC one-word substitution: Custody (legal right to care for a child), Dowry (property/money given at marriage), Bigamy (marrying while already legally married to someone else).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
A group of people travelling together in a van
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Caravan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Caravan" means a group of people, especially traders or pilgrims, travelling together, typically in vehicles such as vans or wagons, often across difficult terrain. (यात्रियों/वाहनों का काफिला)
◦ Example: The caravan of vans made its way slowly across the desert highway.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Gypsies (खानाबदोश लोग): Refers to a nomadic ethnic group of people, not specifically a group travelling together in vans.

• Option 3: Brood (बच्चों का समूह): A group of young birds or animals hatched/born at one time, or informally a person's children collectively; unrelated to travelling in vans.

• Option 4: Constellation (तारामंडल): A group of stars forming a recognisable pattern; unrelated to the given meaning.

NOTE

• "Caravan" is also used in British English for a vehicle (a mobile home towed by a car); in the sense tested here it refers to the group of travellers itself.

• Other collective/group-related one-word substitutions in SSC: Convoy (a group of vehicles travelling together, often for protection), Cavalcade (a procession of vehicles or riders).

question:
Parts of the following sentence have been given as options. Select the option that contains an error.
I think Jeremy will not / have save enough money / by the time / the year ends.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. have save enough money.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes an action that will be completed before another future action/time (the year ending), which requires the Future Perfect Tense.

• Rule — Future Perfect Tense: Subject + will/shall + have + V3 (past participle) + Object

• The segment "have save enough money" wrongly uses the base form "save" instead of the past participle "saved" after "have".
◦ Correct: I think Jeremy will not have saved enough money by the time the year ends.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "the year ends" is correct as written — a subordinate time clause referring to a future event, correctly expressed in the simple present tense (a standard rule for time clauses referring to the future).

• Option 3: "by the time" is correct as written — a standard connector used to introduce a future time clause, often paired with the future perfect tense in the main clause.

• Option 4: "I think Jeremy will not" is correct as written — a grammatically sound opening clause using the simple future with the negative "will not".

NOTE

• With time clauses beginning with "by the time", "before", "when", "after" referring to the future, the verb in the time clause is in the simple present tense, while the main clause commonly uses the future perfect.

• Remember: after any form of "have/has/had", the main verb must be in the past participle (V3) form, never the base form (V1).

The (1)_________ of birds is one of the most fascinating aspects of the natural world. From the soaring flight of eagles to the colourful plumage of parrots, birds have evolved a wide range of (2)_________ to survive and thrive in their environments. One of the most remarkable adaptations is the ability of some birds to migrate over vast distances, often crossing oceans and continents to reach their breeding or wintering grounds. However, many species of birds are facing threats to their survival, such as habitat loss, climate change and (3)_________ by humans. In response, conservation efforts have been put in place to protect these birds and their habitats. This might involve creating protected areas, restoring degraded habitats or reducing the use of pesticides and other harmful chemicals. Another important aspect of bird conservation is (4)_________ populations to track changes over time and identify emerging threats. This can be done through citizen science programmes or through more intensive efforts led by conservation organisations. Ultimately, protecting birds and their habitats is not only important for the birds themselves but also for the broader ecosystems they are a part of, and the many benefits these ecosystems provide to humans, such as clean air and water, and (5)_________ opportunities.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. diversity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank refers to the wide range of different kinds/forms of birds (from eagles to parrots) that is being described as "one of the most fascinating aspects of the natural world". The most appropriate word is "diversity", meaning the state of having a great variety of different types or forms.

• The sentence reads: "The diversity of birds is one of the most fascinating aspects of the natural world." This fits perfectly with the examples that follow — the soaring flight of eagles versus the colourful plumage of parrots — which together illustrate variety among bird species.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "assortment" means a miscellaneous collection of different things; it is normally used for collections of objects, not naturally for describing a category like "birds" in this context.

• Option 2: "variability" refers to the extent to which something varies or changes, often used in a statistical/scientific sense; it does not fit as naturally as "diversity" when describing birds as a subject of fascination.

• Option 3: "multitude" means a large number of something; it emphasizes quantity, not variety of kind, so it does not match the intended meaning as well as "diversity".

NOTE

• "Diversity" is the standard term used to describe variety within a group of living organisms — compare "biodiversity", a commonly used term in environmental science referring to the variety of life in the world or a particular habitat.

• Words like assortment, variety, multitude and diversity are often confused in cloze tests — always check what the surrounding sentence emphasizes (quantity vs. variety vs. kind) before choosing.

• The blank lists a threat to birds' survival, alongside "habitat loss" and "climate change". • The sentence reads: "...many species of birds are facing threats to their survival, such as habitat loss, climate change and exploitation by humans." All three items in this list — habitat loss, climate change, exploitation — are negative threats, which fits the sense of the sentence.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "safeguarding" means protecting from harm; this is a positive action, the opposite of a "threat", so it does not fit the list of dangers.

• Option 2: "preservation" means keeping something safe from harm or decay; again, this is a positive/protective term and cannot logically be listed as a "threat to survival".

• Option 4: "migration" refers to birds' seasonal movement over long distances, which the passage has already described earlier as a "remarkable adaptation", not a threat — so it does not fit as an item in the list of dangers "by humans".

NOTE

• Always check whether the blank needs a positive or negative word based on its surrounding context — here, the list follows "threats to their survival", so only a negative word (a harm caused by humans) can be correct.

• Common threats to wildlife tested in SSC/GK-linked English passages: habitat loss, poaching, exploitation, pollution, climate change, deforestation.
